name: Sterling-Nakamura Clarity SN-11 'Glass Eye'
description:
A precision rifle built around its optics rather than its ballistics. The Clarity SN-11 integrates a multi-spectrum sensor suite that provides the operator with thermal, electromagnetic, and acoustic imaging overlaid onto a BCI-projected heads-up display. The weapon itself fires conventional 6.5mm rounds — it is the targeting system that justifies the price.

Sterling-Nakamura's approach inverts the traditional sniper weapons philosophy. Rather than building a better bullet, they built a better eye. The SN-11's sensor suite can detect targets through walls, identify cyberware signatures from 2km away, and predict target movement using pattern-recognition algorithms that learn from the operator's engagement history.

The Glass Eye has found a niche among intelligence-oriented operators who value the sensor data as much as the weapon's lethality. Some operators reportedly disable the weapon entirely and use the SN-11 purely as a surveillance platform.
legality: Licensed — corporate and military intelligence operators
specifications:
caliber: 6.5mm conventional match-grade
effective_range: 100-1,600 meters (weapon), 3,000 meters (sensor suite)
rate_of_fire: Semi-automatic, 1 round per 2 seconds
capacity: 10-round detachable magazine
weight: 6.8 kg
power_source: Sensor suite: integrated power cell, 8 hours continuous
tactical_use: The Glass Eye is deployed in intelligence-gathering operations where the operator's primary mission is observation and the weapon is a contingency. The multi-spectrum sensor suite provides real-time intelligence that can be shared across a team's BCI network, making the SN-11 operator a force multiplier even without firing a shot. When engagement is necessary, the predictive targeting system eliminates the guesswork from moving-target engagement.
cultural_context: Sterling-Nakamura has positioned the Glass Eye as a tool for professionals who value information over destruction. Their marketing emphasizes restraint and precision — a sharp contrast to Crucible's brutalist philosophy. In the intelligence community, carrying an SN-11 signals that you are in the business of knowing things, and killing is a secondary function.
story_hooks: A Glass Eye operator has been selling the sensor data from their surveillance operations to competing factions — the weapon's recording capability was not supposed to be accessible to the user, but someone cracked the firmware.

Sterling-Nakamura's predictive targeting algorithm has begun flagging individuals as threats before they take any hostile action. The algorithm is either reading intentions or making mistakes — and the consequences of either are disturbing.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, modular precision rifle with an oversized sensor pod dominating the upper receiver. The weapon presents as a fusion of optical instrument and firearm—angular, minimalist, with clean lines interrupted by jutting sensor arrays and thermal vents. The profile suggests surveillance equipment weaponized rather than a traditional sniper platform.
physical_description.dimensions: Overall length: 118 cm | Barrel: 61 cm | Sensor pod: 15 cm × 8 cm × 7 cm | Weight distributed toward the front due to integrated optics
physical_description.weight_description: Noticeably front-heavy (6.8 kg), with the sensor suite pulling the balance forward of the trigger group. Despite the heft, the ergonomic weight distribution feels almost balanced in supported firing positions. Unwieldy when unsupported, but purposefully designed for prone or bipod use.
physical_description.primary_material: Aerospace-grade aluminum chassis with carbon-fiber furniture; sensor pod housing is reinforced polymer composite with embedded thermal dissipation channels
physical_description.finish: Matte gunmetal gray on the receiver with brushed anthracite anodizing. The sensor pod features a subtle iridescent coating that shifts between deep blue and violet under direct light—a practical thermal management finish that also signals the weapon's advanced nature.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray primary | Anthracite accents | Iridescent sensor pod | Accent elements in Sterling-Nakamura's signature violet (BCI interface indicators)
physical_description.grip_texture: Textured polymer grip with subtle radial ridging; cold to the touch. The stock incorporates a soft rubberized cheek rest integrated with a micro-display housing
distinctive_features: Asymmetrical sensor pod mounted on top of receiver with multiple lens apertures facing left, right, and forward
Four small heatsink fins arranged radially around the sensor pod junction
BCI neural interface contact points (three small platinum-coated pads) recessed into the stock beneath a removable access panel
Thermal vent striations along the left side of the lower receiver
Minimalist iron sights—thin, tucked, nearly invisible behind the sensor array
Violet LED indicator cluster (three lights) beneath the rear of the sensor pod, visible only from the operator's position
Modular power cell cartridge accessible via a quick-release panel on the right side of the chassis
Subtle wear patterns on the stock's cheek rest indicating heavy use
Faint circuit-board patterns etched into the aluminum receiver as manufacturer branding
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: STERLING-NAKAMURA corporate logo stamped in micro-text along the left side of the lower receiver, barely visible unless light catches it. Serial number engraved on the power cell housing. Model designation 'SN-11' printed in small sans-serif font on the sensor pod itself. No overt branding—the design language speaks louder than logos.
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained and field-worn; the finish shows light scuffing on the receiver from tactical use and careful handling. The sensor pod surface is pristine—protected obsessively by operators who understand the weapon's true value lies in its eyes, not its trigger. The stock shows patina from repeated contact with body armor and BCI neural interfaces.
